note.label: TIMES OF TEMPTATION

precepts.why:
This shows what happens to the young men who faint at the head of the streets. Of the three men before the king, the first “had spoken of the strength of wine”, and here it is speaking of actual liquor: “how exceeding strong is wine! it causeth all men to err that drink it.” It causes all men to sin that drink it to excess.

“It maketh the mind of the king and of the fatherless child to be all one; of the bondman and of the freeman, of the poor man and of the rich.” The influence of liquor puts a king in the same mindset as a fatherless child; whatever their status, drunk to excess, all men behave alike. “It turneth also every thought into jollity and mirth, so that a man remembereth neither sorrow nor debt”: when black folks can’t pay the bills, they buy beer or liquor and drink their worries away. “So that a man remembereth neither king nor governor”: you forget the authority, the police, all the authorities of the world. “And it maketh to speak all things by talents”: it is a truth serum; you say things you would never say sober. Careless, carefree, open and honest.

“And when they are in their cups, they forget their love both to friends and brethren, and a little after draw out swords”: no loyalty to friends or family, and then violent. “But when they are from the wine, they remember not what they have done.” Like the fifteen-year-old who killed another boy and cried when the judge denied his parole: there was no thought of consequence beforehand, because the fatherless child is carefree, with no care for authority, open and honest enough to rap about what he did. Then he wants his lawyer.

“Is not wine the strongest, that enforceth to do thus?” That goes back to Isaiah, the sons lying in the streets as a wild bull in a net. The child who walks around with no father at home has the same attributes: no care for authority, happy, jolly, carefree, open, honest, forgetting what he did, crying in the end, not loyal to friends or family, killing his brother, going against his parents. Fatherless children are like drunkards.

note.label: These Are Not Defiled With Women Part 2

precepts.why:
“Declare unto us your mind concerning the writings. Then began the first, who had spoken of the strength of wine”. He is declaring the strength of wine. “It turneth also every thought into jollity and mirth, so that a man remembereth neither sorrow nor debt.” Jollity is joy: wine turns your thoughts into joyful thoughts, a time of gladness. It is supposed to make you merry, so you forget sorrow and the debt you are in.

But past a certain limit you become violent and your whole spirit changes, and that is the time to stop. “And when they are in their cups, they forget their love both to friends and brethren, and a little after draw out swords.” All of a sudden the brother you were drinking with is about to fight you; you forget that is your brother because of liquor. Many of us know people in our neighbourhoods and families who got drunk and nearly put each other to death, and here it is in the Holy Bible.

If you know you are an angry drunk, stop drinking. If you know you are a sobbing, weeping ass brother, stop drinking. If the liquor makes you start pouring out your heart and making everybody sorrowful, keep your sorrow to yourself and stop drinking.

points: Then the three young men that were of the guard that kept the king's body spake one to another: these three were the king's bodyguard. Let me fill in the gap: the king set forth a contest; whoever gives the wisest saying about what is the strongest, I will give you wealth, fame and fortune, and you can sit beside me. The three bodyguards accepted the challenge.
The first wrote, Wine is the strongest. The second wrote, The king is strongest. The third wrote, Women are strongest: but above all things Truth beareth away the victory. The third was Zerubbabel.
So in order to be one of them, you had to understand nobility.
You had to have extreme physical endurance.
People had to see you at war.

Unwavering personal loyalty to the monarch. To the king. Now, I sit back and I think, why would Zerubbabel do what the Persian king said? You got to think about it. Let's say you're this top fighter, but the rest of the brothers and sisters are not. And they got the knives to everybody's throat: if you don't give up, we kill everybody. What would you do as a top warrior?

Now, how many of y'all saw the movie The Usual Suspects? So now that was an extreme case. Now we're talking about the Persians or Babylon taking everybody in captivity. They got the whole nation tied up.
So Zerubbabel, obviously he didn't fight, because he said, You know what? If I fight, they all going to die. I might live, but they going to die. So he became the king's bodyguard.
